name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q01 - Impulse calculation from position time graph

questiontext.text:
The figure below shows the position-time (\( x-t \)) graph of a particle of mass \( 4\text{ kg} \) moving along the \( x \)-axis in one dimension:

What is the magnitude and sign of the impulse imparted to the particle at time \( t = 4\text{ s} \)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the particle, \( m = 4\text{ kg} \).
From the graph:

  • For \( t < 0 \), the position is \( x = 0 \), so the particle is at rest with velocity \( v = 0 \).
  • For the interval \( 0 < t < 4\text{ s} \), the graph is a straight line passing through \( (0, 0) \) and \( (4\text{ s}, 3\text{ m}) \).
  • For \( t > 4\text{ s} \), the position remains constant at \( x = 3\text{ m} \), so the particle is again at rest with velocity \( v = 0 \).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The velocity in one-dimensional motion is given by the slope of the position-time graph: \[ v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \] Linear momentum is defined as \( p = mv \).
Impulse \( J \) imparted to a particle is equal to the change in its linear momentum: \[ J = \Delta p = p_{\text{final}} - p_{\text{initial}} = m(v_{\text{final}} - v_{\text{initial}}) \]

Step 3: Velocity and Momentum before \( t = 4\text{ s} \)
Just before \( t = 4\text{ s} \) (in the time interval \( 0 < t < 4\text{ s} \)), the velocity of the particle is the constant slope of the straight-line segment: \[ v_1 = \frac{3\text{ m} - 0\text{ m}}{4\text{ s} - 0\text{ s}} = 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1} \] The linear momentum of the particle just before \( t = 4\text{ s} \) is: \[ p_1 = m v_1 = 4\text{ kg} \times 0.75\text{ m s}^{-1} = 3\text{ kg m s}^{-1} = 3\text{ N s} \]

Step 4: Velocity and Momentum after \( t = 4\text{ s} \)
Just after \( t = 4\text{ s} \) (for \( t > 4\text{ s} \)), the position is constant at \( x = 3\text{ m} \), which means the slope is zero: \[ v_2 = 0\text{ m s}^{-1} \] The linear momentum of the particle just after \( t = 4\text{ s} \) is: \[ p_2 = m v_2 = 4\text{ kg} \times 0 = 0\text{ N s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The impulse imparted to the particle at \( t = 4\text{ s} \) is: \[ J = p_2 - p_1 = 0\text{ N s} - 3\text{ N s} = -3\text{ N s} \] The negative sign indicates that the retarding impulsive force acts in the negative \( x \)-direction to bring the particle to rest. Therefore, the impulse imparted is \( -3\text{ N s} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q02 - Impulse ratio and force direction on wall

questiontext.text:
Two identical billiard balls, each of mass \( m \), strike a rigid vertical wall with speed \( u \) and rebound with the same speed \( u \), as shown in the figure below:

In Case (a), the ball strikes normally to the wall. In Case (b), the ball strikes at an angle of \( 30^\circ \) to the normal to the wall. What is the ratio of the magnitude of impulse imparted to the ball by the wall in Case (a) to that in Case (b), and what is the direction of the force exerted on the wall by the ball in each case?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Coordinate Setup
Mass of each ball = \( m \), initial speed = \( u \), final speed = \( u \).
Let the vertical wall lie along the \( y \)-axis, with the normal to the wall directed along the horizontal \( x \)-axis pointing away from the wall (outward).
The impulse imparted to the ball by the wall is equal to the change in momentum vector of the ball: \[ \mathbf{J} = \Delta \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_{\text{final}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{initial}} \]

Step 2: Impulse in Case (a) (Normal Incidence)
The ball travels along the positive \( x \)-axis towards the wall and rebounds along the negative \( x \)-axis:

  • Initial momentum: \( p_{x,\text{initial}} = mu \), \( p_{y,\text{initial}} = 0 \)
  • Final momentum: \( p_{x,\text{final}} = -mu \), \( p_{y,\text{final}} = 0 \)
Change in momentum of the ball: \[ \Delta p_x = -mu - mu = -2mu, \quad \Delta p_y = 0 \] Magnitude of impulse on the ball in Case (a): \[ J_a = 2mu \] The force on the ball by the wall is directed along the negative \( x \)-direction. By Newton's third law, the force on the wall by the ball is directed along the positive \( x \)-direction, which is normal to the wall.

Step 3: Impulse in Case (b) (Oblique Incidence at \( 30^\circ \))
Resolving velocity along and parallel to the wall:

  • Initial momentum: \( p_{x,\text{initial}} = mu \cos 30^\circ \), \( p_{y,\text{initial}} = -mu \sin 30^\circ \)
  • Final momentum: \( p_{x,\text{final}} = -mu \cos 30^\circ \), \( p_{y,\text{final}} = -mu \sin 30^\circ \)
Notice that the parallel component \( p_y \) does not change because the wall is frictionless. The perpendicular component reverses direction.
Change in momentum: \[ \Delta p_x = -mu \cos 30^\circ - mu \cos 30^\circ = -2mu \cos 30^\circ, \quad \Delta p_y = 0 \] Magnitude of impulse in Case (b): \[ J_b = 2mu \cos 30^\circ = 2mu \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \sqrt{3}mu \] Since \( \Delta p_y = 0 \), the impulse and the force on the ball are purely along the negative \( x \)-direction. By Newton's third law, the force on the wall by the ball is purely along the positive \( x \)-direction, which is normal to the wall.

Step 4: Ratio of Impulses
The ratio of the magnitude of impulse in Case (a) to Case (b) is: \[ \frac{J_a}{J_b} = \frac{2mu}{\sqrt{3}mu} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The ratio of the impulses is \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \), and the force exerted on the wall is normal to the wall in both cases.

answer.text: Ratio is \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \); normal to the wall in Case (a) and inclined at \( 30^\circ \) to the normal in Case (b)
Ratio is \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \); normal to the wall in both cases
Ratio is \( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \); normal to the wall in both cases
Ratio is \( 2 \); normal to the wall in both cases

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q03 - Tension and inclination of deflected suspended rope

questiontext.text:
A mass of \( 6\text{ kg} \) (weight \( W = 60\text{ N} \)) is suspended from the ceiling by a light inextensible rope of length \( 2\text{ m} \). A horizontal force of \( 50\text{ N} \) is applied at the midpoint P of the rope, deflecting it as shown in the diagram below:

When the entire system is in static equilibrium, what are the angle \( \theta \) that the upper segment of the rope makes with the vertical and the tension \( T_1 \) in this upper segment? (Take \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass suspended, \( m = 6\text{ kg} \).
Weight of the mass, \( W = mg = 6\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 60\text{ N} \).
Horizontal applied force at point P, \( F = 50\text{ N} \).
The rope is light (massless), so tension is uniform within each straight section.

Step 2: Equilibrium of the Suspended Weight
Consider the vertical equilibrium of the hanging block of weight \( W \): The upward tension in the lower segment of the rope is \( T_2 \), and the downward gravitational force is \( W = 60\text{ N} \). Since the block is at rest: \[ T_2 = W = 60\text{ N} \]

Step 3: Equilibrium of Midpoint P
Point P is acted upon by three concurrent forces:

  • Tension \( T_1 \) pulling upward and leftward at angle \( \theta \) to the vertical.
  • Horizontal force \( F = 50\text{ N} \) pulling to the right.
  • Tension \( T_2 = 60\text{ N} \) pulling vertically downward.
Resolving forces at point P along the horizontal and vertical directions: \[ \sum F_x = 0 \implies F - T_1 \\sin\\theta = 0 \implies T_1 \sin\theta = 50\text{ N} \] \[ \sum F_y = 0 \implies T_1 \cos\theta - T_2 = 0 \implies T_1 \cos\theta = 60\text{ N} \]

Step 4: Calculation of Angle \( \theta \) and Tension \( T_1 \)
Dividing the horizontal equilibrium equation by the vertical equilibrium equation: \[ \tan\theta = \frac{T_1 \sin\theta}{T_1 \cos\theta} = \frac{50}{60} = \frac{5}{6} \] \[ \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \approx 40^\circ \] Squaring and adding both equilibrium equations to determine \( T_1 \): \[ (T_1 \sin\theta)^2 + (T_1 \cos\theta)^2 = 50^2 + 60^2 \] \[ T_1^2 (\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) = 2500 + 3600 = 6100 \] \[ T_1 = \sqrt{6100} = 10\sqrt{61}\text{ N} \approx 78.1\text{ N} \]

Step 5: Final Answer
The tension in the upper segment is \( T_1 = 10\sqrt{61}\text{ N} \) and the angle with the vertical is \( \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q04 - Angle of repose and self adjusting friction

questiontext.text:
A block of mass \( 4\text{ kg} \) rests on an inclined plane whose angle of inclination \( \theta \) can be varied, as depicted in the figure below:

When the inclination \( \theta \) is gradually increased from zero, the block is found to just begin sliding down when \( \theta = 15^\circ \). Taking \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \), determine the coefficient of static friction \( \mu_s \) between the block and the surface, and the magnitude of the actual frictional force \( f_s \) acting on the block when the plane is set at an inclination of \( \theta = 10^\circ \).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Limiting Equilibrium Condition
Mass of the block, \( m = 4\text{ kg} \).
Acceleration due to gravity, \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \).
Weight of the block, \( W = mg = 4 \times 10 = 40\text{ N} \).
Angle of repose (angle of impending sliding), \( \theta_{\max} = 15^\circ \).

Step 2: Determining the Coefficient of Static Friction
On an inclined plane, resolving the weight along and perpendicular to the inclined plane:

  • Normal reaction force: \( N = mg \cos\theta \)
  • Downslope gravitational pull: \( F_{\text{down}} = mg \sin\theta \)
  • Static friction acts upslope: \( f_s \)
At the critical angle of repose \( \theta_{\max} = 15^\circ \), static friction reaches its maximum limiting value: \[ f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg \cos\theta_{\max} \] Equating forces along the incline at impending sliding: \[ mg \sin\theta_{\max} = \mu_s mg \cos\theta_{\max} \implies \mu_s = \tan\theta_{\max} = \tan 15^\circ \approx 0.27 \]

Step 3: Actual Static Frictional Force at \( \theta = 10^\circ \)
Since the inclination angle \( \theta = 10^\circ \) is strictly less than the angle of repose \( 15^\circ \), the block does not slide and remains at rest.
Static friction is a self-adjusting force that exactly balances the net applied force attempting to cause motion. Therefore, the actual static friction is not equal to its maximum possible value, but is exactly equal to the downslope component of gravity: \[ f_s = mg \sin 10^\circ = 40 \sin 10^\circ\text{ N} \approx 40 \times 0.1736\text{ N} = 6.95\text{ N} \]

Step 4: Check Limiting Maximum Value
The maximum available static friction at \( 10^\circ \) is: \[ f_{s,\max} = \mu_s mg \cos 10^\circ = 0.27 \times 40 \times \cos 10^\circ \approx 10.6\text{ N} \] Since \( 6.95\text{ N} < 10.6\text{ N} \), the required friction is well within the available capacity, confirming the block is in static equilibrium.

Step 5: Final Answer
The coefficient of static friction is \( \mu_s = \tan 15^\circ \approx 0.27 \) and the actual frictional force is \( f_s = 40 \sin 10^\circ\text{ N} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q05 - Acceleration and tension in trolley hanging system

questiontext.text:
In the trolley and hanging block arrangement shown below, a trolley of mass \( 20\text{ kg} \) rests on a rough horizontal surface and is connected via a light inextensible string passing over a smooth frictionless pulley to a hanging block of mass \( 3\text{ kg} \):

The coefficient of kinetic friction between the trolley and the horizontal surface is \( \mu_k = 0.04 \). Taking \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \), calculate the magnitude of the acceleration \( a \) of the system and the tension \( T \) in the connecting string.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Normal Reaction on the Trolley
Mass of trolley, \( M = 20\text{ kg} \).
Mass of hanging block, \( m = 3\text{ kg} \).
Coefficient of kinetic friction, \( \mu_k = 0.04 \).
Acceleration due to gravity, \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \).
For the trolley on the horizontal surface, vertical equilibrium gives: \[ N = Mg = 20\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 200\text{ N} \] The kinetic frictional force opposing the motion of the trolley is: \[ f_k = \mu_k N = 0.04 \times 200\text{ N} = 8\text{ N} \]

Step 2: Equation of Motion for the Hanging Block
The hanging block experiences downward gravitational force \( mg = 3 \times 10 = 30\text{ N} \) and upward string tension \( T \).
Applying Newton's second law along the downward direction: \[ mg - T = ma \implies 30 - T = 3a \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)} \]

Step 3: Equation of Motion for the Trolley
The trolley experiences rightward string tension \( T \) and opposing kinetic friction \( f_k = 8\text{ N} \).
Applying Newton's second law along the horizontal direction: \[ T - f_k = Ma \implies T - 8 = 20a \quad \text{--- (Equation 2)} \]

Step 4: Solving for Acceleration \( a \) and String Tension \( T \)
Adding Equation 1 and Equation 2 eliminates tension \( T \): \[ (30 - T) + (T - 8) = 3a + 20a \] \[ 22 = 23a \implies a = \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 0.957\text{ m s}^{-2} \] Substituting the value of \( a \) back into Equation 1 to find \( T \): \[ T = 30 - 3a = 30 - 3\left(\frac{22}{23}\right) = \frac{690 - 66}{23} = \frac{624}{23}\text{ N} \approx 27.13\text{ N} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying with Equation 2: \[ T - 8 = \frac{624}{23} - \frac{184}{23} = \frac{440}{23} = 20 \times \frac{22}{23} = 20a \] The results are consistent. The acceleration of the system is \( \frac{22}{23}\text{ m s}^{-2} \) and the tension in the string is \( \frac{624}{23}\text{ N} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_LAWS_OF_MOTION_DIAGRAM_IMAGE_Q06 - Action reaction forces on yielding floor system

questiontext.text:
A wooden block of mass \( 2\text{ kg} \) rests on a soft horizontal floor. When an iron cylinder of mass \( 25\text{ kg} \) is placed on top of the block, the soft floor yields steadily, causing the block and cylinder to sink together with a downward acceleration of \( 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2} \), as shown in the diagram below:

Taking \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \), determine the downward force exerted by the wooden block on the floor (action) (i) before the cylinder is placed, and (ii) while the floor yields steadily under the combined load.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the wooden block, \( m_1 = 2\text{ kg} \).
Mass of the iron cylinder, \( m_2 = 25\text{ kg} \).
Acceleration due to gravity, \( g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2} \).
Downward acceleration during floor yielding, \( a = 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2} \).

Step 2: Action Force Before Yielding (Block Alone at Rest)
Before the cylinder is placed, the block of mass \( 2\text{ kg} \) is at rest on the floor.
The forces acting on the block are:

  • Downward gravitational pull: \( W_1 = m_1 g = 2\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 20\text{ N} \)
  • Upward normal force exerted by the floor: \( R \)
By Newton's first law, since the block is in static equilibrium: \[ R - W_1 = 0 \implies R = 20\text{ N} \] By Newton's third law, the action force exerted on the floor by the block is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the normal force exerted by the floor on the block: \[ F_{\text{action}} = 20\text{ N directed vertically downward.} \]

Step 3: Action Force During Steady Yielding (Combined System Accelerating Downward)
When the cylinder is placed on the block, treat the block and cylinder together as a single composite system of total mass: \[ M = m_1 + m_2 = 2\text{ kg} + 25\text{ kg} = 27\text{ kg} \] The total downward gravitational force on the system is: \[ W_{\text{total}} = M g = 27\text{ kg} \times 10\text{ m s}^{-2} = 270\text{ N} \] The floor exerts an upward normal reaction \( R' \) on the base of the wooden block.
The system accelerates downwards with \( a = 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2} \).
Applying Newton's second law to the composite system: \[ M g - R' = M a \] \[ 270\text{ N} - R' = 27\text{ kg} \times 0.1\text{ m s}^{-2} = 2.7\text{ N} \] \[ R' = 270 - 2.7 = 267.3\text{ N} \]

Step 4: Application of Newton's Third Law
The upward normal force exerted by the yielding floor on the block is \( R' = 267.3\text{ N} \).
By Newton's third law, the downward action force exerted by the block on the floor is equal in magnitude: \[ F'_{\text{action}} = 267.3\text{ N directed vertically downward.} \]

Step 5: Final Answer
The downward action force on the floor is \( 20\text{ N} \) before the cylinder is placed, and \( 267.3\text{ N} \) after the floor yields.

answer.text: \( 20\text{ N} \) initially, and \( 270\text{ N} \) after yielding
\( 20\text{ N} \) initially, and \( 267.3\text{ N} \) after yielding
\( 20\text{ N} \) initially, and \( 272.7\text{ N} \) after yielding
\( 0\text{ N} \) initially, and \( 267.3\text{ N} \) after yielding
